title: L'imaginaire du sabbat: Édition critique des textes les plus anciens (1430 c.–1440 c.)
author: Martine Ostorero, Agostino Paravicini Bagliani, Kathrin Utz Tremp (eds.)
original_title: L'imaginaire du sabbat: Édition critique des textes les plus anciens (1430 c.–1440 c.)
original_publisher: Université de Lausanne (Cahiers lausannois d'histoire médiévale, 26), Lausanne
subject_focus: Critical edition with scholarly analysis of the five earliest surviving texts documenting organized sabbath doctrine (c.1430–c.1440), establishing the Alpine origin and 1420s–1440s crystallization of the composite witch stereotype.
summary: L'imaginaire du sabbat is the definitive critical edition of the five texts that contain the earliest known descriptions of the organized witches' sabbath — the composite diabolical gathering that became the core of the early modern witch stereotype. The texts, all dating to approximately 1430–1440 and originating in Alpine or sub-Alpine contexts (Savoy, Dauphiné, the Valais, the western Swiss Confederation), are: the anonymous Errores Gazariorum (c.1436), Claude Tholosan's Ut magorum et maleficiorum errores (c.1436), Hans Fründ's chronicle account of Valais prosecutions (1428), the anonymous Account of the Vauderie of Lyon, and Nider's relevant sections of the Formicarius (c.1437). Each text receives a critical Latin or French edition with full scholarly introduction, apparatus, and French translation; the volume as a whole includes introductory chapters establishing the historical and intellectual context. The editors demonstrate collectively that these five texts — geographically concentrated, temporally clustered, and mutually independent in their key elements — represent the crystallization of the composite witch stereotype in a specific Alpine milieu in the 1420s–1440s.
scholarly_significance:
L'imaginaire du sabbat is the single most important scholarly resource for understanding the formation of the composite witch stereotype and the Alpine origins of sabbath doctrine. Its philological and historical precision transformed the field: before this volume, the earliest phase of stereotype formation was documented only through secondary-source analysis; the critical editions here provide the primary textual foundation for all subsequent work on the composite concept's origin.

  The volume definitively established the scholarly consensus on the crystallization chronology: the composite witch stereotype — combining maleficium, demonic pact, apostasy, sabbath, and flight — took coherent form in the Alpine localities of the 1420s–1440s, not (as older historiography assumed) in the late fifteenth century with the Malleus Maleficarum. The five texts documented here predate the Malleus by half a century and show the composite concept already substantially formed.

  The geographical concentration of the earliest texts is itself analytically significant: all five originate in Alpine or sub-Alpine environments where the ecclesiastical jurisdictions of Savoy, the western Confederation, and Dauphiné overlapped, where Waldensian prosecution had recently intensified, and where secular and ecclesiastical prosecution authorities were unusually active. The editors analyze how this specific local environment enabled the synthesis of pre-existing elements — heresy accusations against Waldensians, folk beliefs about night-flight, maleficium prosecutions — into the composite stereotype.

  Michael Bailey's Battling Demons (2003) and this volume are complementary: Bailey provides the intellectual and reforming context (focused on Nider) while L'imaginaire du sabbat provides the philological editions of all five foundational texts. Together they constitute the scholarly foundation for the database's composite-witch-stereotype-formation entries.

  Stuart Clark (Thinking with Demons, 1997) had partly anticipated the Alpine origin argument; L'imaginaire du sabbat provided the documentary foundation that Clark's analysis required. The volume is cited by Hutton (The Witch, 2017) as essential for the formation narrative.

key_arguments.concept: Alpine crystallization of the composite stereotype
key_arguments.claim: The composite witch stereotype crystallized in the Alpine and sub-Alpine regions of western Europe (Savoy, Valais, Dauphiné, western Switzerland) in the 1420s–1440s, at least half a century before the Malleus Maleficarum and in a specific geopolitical context where Waldensian heresy prosecution, secular and ecclesiastical jurisdictions, and Alpine folk beliefs converged.

key_arguments.concept: Five foundational texts as independent witnesses
key_arguments.claim: The five texts edited in this volume — Errores Gazariorum, Tholosan's treatise, Fründ's chronicle, the Vauderie de Lyon account, and Nider's Formicarius — originated independently in the same geographical area and time period; their convergence on the core elements of sabbath doctrine (nocturnal gathering, demonic pact, flight, orgies, infanticide) demonstrates that the composite stereotype crystallized through multiple independent appropriations of a shared conceptual development rather than through a single authoritative text.

The composite witch stereotype drew heavily on the existing Waldensian heresy prosecution template, including the term 'vaudois' (used interchangeably with 'witch' in several texts) and the organizational model of a secret sect meeting at night for blasphemous ritual; the construction of the witch as a sectarian heretic rather than an individual malefactor owed more to Waldensian prosecution practice than to any theological innovation.

The composite stereotype emerged through the accumulation and synthesis of pre-existing elements — Roman law maleficium, canon law apostasy and demonic pact, folk beliefs about night-flight and transformation, heresy prosecution templates — rather than through a sudden conceptual breakthrough; the Alpine context of the 1420s–1440s provided the conditions in which these elements could be synthesized into a coherent and prosecutable composite.

relation_to_database: L'imaginaire du sabbat is the primary source for database entries on the composite witch stereotype's formation, the Alpine origin of sabbath doctrine, and the early-fifteenth-century crystallization event. Timeline entries covering the 1428–1440 period draw on this volume for the specific texts and their dating. The Errores Gazariorum, Tholosan's treatise, and Fründ's chronicle are cited in individual timeline entries.
scholarly_disagreement: The Alpine crystallization thesis established by this volume has been broadly accepted. Debate continues about the precise mechanism of synthesis: Richard Kieckhefer (argument in Forbidden Rites, 1997 and subsequent articles) emphasizes the role of popular belief traditions alongside learned clerical synthesis, which the Lausanne editors perhaps underweigh. Bailey (Battling Demons, 2003) and Norman Cohn (Europe's Inner Demons, 1975) debate the relative weight of the Waldensian template versus novel synthesis; the Lausanne editors' emphasis on Waldensian prosecution as template aligns more closely with Cohn than with Bailey's reforming-context analysis. The French-language format of this critical edition has limited its reception in Anglophone scholarship, where it is known primarily through secondary citation.
